summary:
What if farmers could know which crop rotation is best for their fields as the climate changes?

Field Shift is a free web app that turns NASA climate data, satellite observations, and soil information into practical crop rotation recommendations.

Farmers simply select their field on a map. The app retrieves historical crop data and analyzes 20 years of weather patterns, including rainfall, drought risk, frost dates, and extreme heat, alongside local soil conditions.

It compares the current rotation with three alternatives, allowing farmers to prioritize water conservation, soil health, nitrogen, erosion, pest management, forage, and market opportunities. Each option also includes estimated gross margins per acre.

Interactive 3D visualizations show root growth and soil cover throughout the year, while satellite data from NASA HLS, MODIS, and SMAP, combined with machine learning trained on Landsat and Sentinel-2 observations, helps examine real field conditions and historical crop patterns.

Every recommendation explains its reasoning, identifies its data sources, and highlights uncertainties that require local verification. Available in English and French.

Field Shift turns NASA science into actionable insights, helping farmers prepare for a changing climate while keeping every decision in their hands.
details:
One click. Twenty years of NASA data. Your field, your call.

Every farmer asks the same question: which rotation fits my field as the weather shifts? Field Shift answers it for their own field, in minutes.

How it works
Click your field and the app fills in what you've grown, using USDA and AAFC crop maps. It reads 20 years of NASA POWER weather and the local soil for that exact spot, rules out what frost or water make impossible, and compares your rotation with three alternatives on the goals you choose. You get one clear suggestion, a smaller first step, and every option side by side. Each option comes with its gross margin, its evidence, and what to check before you change.

What satellites revealed
On our Iowa example field, NASA satellites show the soil lay bare through 18 heavy-rain months from 2019 to 2024. Keeping corn and soybean and adding a winter rye cover takes the bare months from about 7 a year to none.

Why it matters

  • Field-level guidance from free public data, with no account or API keys.
  • Every number names its source, and every gap is stated plainly.
  • In English or French, on a laptop at the kitchen table or a phone in the field.
  • The farmer always makes the final call.

What makes it different

  • It starts from the farmer's decision and current rotation, not from satellite layers.
  • A 3D view brings the seasons to life: living roots against bare soil, month by month.
  • AI is used only where it can be checked. Our crop model reads the crop from satellite greenness, scores 88.5% on seasons and places it never saw, and checks the farmer's crop history.

Built with

  • NASA data: POWER, HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2), MODIS and SMAP.
  • Code: Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, three.js and MapLibre.
  • Models: XGBoost and TimesFM 2.5.
  • Deployment: Vercel.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code.

What guided us: scientific honesty, plain language, respect for what farmers know, free access, coverage of Canada and the U.S., and accessibility.
